item.title: G-Player 0.4.4
item.description:
• Epic's own launcher opens on G-Player Wine. The Epic Games Launcher no longer stops at its loading screen: it reaches Epic's sign-in page. G-Player starts it on G-Player Wine with Epic's own web helper (the Chromium helper wrapper made its network service crash again and again there) and on DXMT, also when you have added D3DMetal, whatever its library entry says: DXVK and WineD3D don't open it, and with D3DMetal its web view can't start its GPU process, so it renders in software and feels sluggish. A space that already has the wrapper in Epic's helper gets Epic's helper back before the next start, and nothing is deleted. An Epic Games Launcher space on Wine Staging is offered Move to G-Player Wine… on its page, and new ones are made on G-Player Wine. A game from Epic's launcher that you play in G-Player goes through the launcher (G-Player starts EpicGamesLauncher.exe with the game's link), so while the launcher is open the game inherits its DXMT: a DirectX 12 game, which needs D3DMetal, may not run then. Quit the launcher first and G-Player starts it with the game's own graphics, which makes the launcher itself run on them (D3DMetal renders its web view in software). Get Apps has one Epic Games card with both ways to Epic's games: Epic Games Launcher (recommended), and Without the launcher, which is faster and goes through Legendary.
  • Epic's launcher installs Epic Online Services. Games can be installed from Epic's launcher now: its first start no longer ends with "Epic Online Services is not installed" (error II-E1007). Epic's installer for it has .NET steps, and G-Player kept .NET off to spare you Wine's own download prompts. For this launcher G-Player now brings Wine Mono (.NET for Wine, 10.4.1, the version G-Player Wine expects): the first time you open the launcher (or set it up) it downloads Wine Mono (40 MB, checked against a pinned SHA-256, with progress and a Stop in the sidebar) into G-Player Wine, where it takes about 245 MB, and adds it to the launcher's space once; the launcher then starts with .NET on. Nothing else gets it: other apps and games start as before, and Wine Staging has none. In a bottle of another app it asks first, like every change G-Player makes there. A launcher that is already open keeps what it started with: quit it and open it again.
  • Epic's launcher can install games. It waits for a file change notification before it installs, and G-Player Wine's wineserver had none on a Mac: Install did nothing. G-Player puts a wineserver built with file change notifications (libinotify) into G-Player Wine 26.3.0-2 by itself, keeping the engine's own one next to it. Quit G-Player and Epic's launcher once after updating.
  • Epic's launcher stays signed in. It signs its Epic Online Services token requests with an ECDSA key, which G-Player Wine's Wine couldn't make: every request failed, the launcher went offline after a while, and a game started then said it needs a signed-in launcher. G-Player puts Wine's own fix for it (ncrypt with ECDSA P-256) into G-Player Wine 26.3.0-2, keeping the engine's files next to it.
  • Epic games without Epic's launcher. The card's second way, Without the launcher, opens the Epic Games page over Get Apps (with a back button). It signs you in on Epic's own page (with Epic, Google, Apple or whatever you use: G-Player never sees your password, and the window keeps nothing) and lists the games your account owns. Install puts a game into a space of its own, "Epic Games", on G-Player Wine, one at a time, with progress and a Stop in the sidebar; that space is in Spaces like any other and links back to the page with Your Epic Library, and the games in it show in All Games; Play starts it through G-Player's own launch (graphics, components, automatic retry), asking Epic for a one-time code each time, or starting offline when Epic can't be reached; Uninstall… and Sign Out undo them. It works through [Legendary](https://github.com/legendary-gl/legendary) 0.21.1 (GPL-3.0), an open-source Epic client that is not part of G-Player: the first time you sign in, G-Player downloads it (15 MB) from its GitHub release and checks it against a pinned SHA-256, and runs it as a separate program with settings of its own in the library's Tools folder. The one-time code a game is started with is hidden in launch logs and messages. Before the first Epic game goes into the library, G-Player keeps library.json as library.json.before-epic-, because a G-Player from before Epic Games takes a library with an Epic game in it for damaged (use the copy to go back); from now on a game this version can't read is kept as it is and left out instead of breaking the library. Moving the library leaves Epic games marked "Files not found" with Repair or Remove… instead of dropping them. Not in this version: game updates, verify and repair, cloud saves, Epic's overlay and games' prerequisite installers; games with EasyAntiCheat or BattlEye don't run on a Mac.
  • G-Player updates itself. G-Player › Check for Updates… looks for a newer version and installs it, so you no longer download the disk image by hand. The second time G-Player opens it asks whether to check by itself (once a day); Settings › General turns that on or off. G-Player asks GitHub for the list of versions and sends nothing about your Mac, and an update installs only if it is signed with G-Player's own update key. This version is the first that does it: install 0.4.4 from its disk image once, and the next ones come by themselves.
  • Every engine install and update writes what it went through, and how it ended, to Logs in the library, so an update that failed in the background can be looked into later.
